🎯 Serving Architecture Pareto Frontier (Latency vs Throughput)
Trade-off curve between First-Token Latency (TTFT seconds) and Token Generation Throughput (tok/s) across topologies at 128K & 1M context.
Executive TakeawayTP4/PP4 occupies the optimal Pareto frontier corner: delivering lowest TTFT (1.71s at 128K, 28.57s at 1M) and highest cluster generation efficiency (31.0 to 104.2 tok/s).
⏱️ End-to-End Wall-Time Budget Breakdown (§4.17 Architecture Spectrum)
Percentage allocation of request turn time from short context (8K) to extreme prompt length (1M tokens).
AUDITED DECOMPOSITION
Regime Shift8K serving is 54% communication/barrier-bound. As prompt length expands to 1M tokens, compute and memory bandwidth account for 83% of wall time.

Known before metrics are loaded.
Application E2E: GCP_NATIVE + configured-100G + configured-20G measured (119 completed runs). All native topology, long-context, scheduler/KV, compute, NCCL, telemetry and profiler evidence surfaced when present.

Not established / Unresolved: Application E2E at 50G/10G, local physical 2×10GbE equivalence, two-node decode profiles (single-node graphs-on decode profiles exist; multi-node decode profiles deferred), and minimum production bandwidth threshold.

📡 Prefill Communication Share by Prompt Length — The Number Behind "Comm Isn't the HW Bottleneck" (§4.4)
An 8K prefill chunk executes 55 AllReduces of 8,192 × 2,304 × 2 B = 37.7 MB. nccl-tests (TP4 native): 19.0 µs @ 16 KiB, 17.4 GB/s algbw @ 256 MiB → α-β time ≈ 2.19 ms. In eager prefill capture (tp4_prefill), 880 prefill-chunk calls = 2.18 ms/call (α-β estimate within 1%). Chunk compute scales quadratically with prefix; AllReduce communication cost does not.

Hardware Bottleneck Quantification: On this PCIe host (26 GB/s ring busbw, no NVLink), intra-node TP prefill spends 16–57% of first token in AllReduce depending on prompt length, while cross-node TP16 spends 77% (12 usable ranks). For PP boundaries, SendRecv waits consume only 8–22% of kernel time (§4.7). These three numbers answer where faster fabric helps: TP within a node for short prompts, yes; PP across nodes, no.

🚫 What Not To Do
Promote as measured lessons only when performance characterization evidence supports them
Do not choose topology from peak tokens/sec alone.
Do not call admission success production capacity.
Do not assume “fits in VRAM” means usable latency.
Do not assume prefill and decode prefer the same topology.
Do not extrapolate 128K behavior linearly to 1M.
Do not extrapolate beyond the measured Native / configured-100G / configured-20G points; do not infer 50G/10G application behavior or local 2×10GbE equivalence without runs.
Do not infer NCCL/PP causality from E2E latency alone.
Do not compare unmatched workload conditions.
Do not use profiler-instrumented latency as normal benchmark latency.
Do not treat CUTLASS reference as model-kernel efficiency.
Do not tune scheduler knobs blindly if another subsystem dominates.
Do not render missing / unresolved evidence as zero.

Dual RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (16× 96GB GPUs)
GCP Native (173.6G) · Capped 100G (56.8G) · Capped 20G (16.5G)
🌟 Section 1: First Screen — Three Hero Discoveries Rendered in exact order: 1. Fabric Exposure Fingerprint (#2) · 2. Concurrency Value Destruction (#3) · 3. Long-Context Resource-Pressure Shift (#1)
🏛 Executive Architecture Synthesis (Section 22 Mandate)
“This campaign shows that deployment behavior is regime-dependent, not described by one throughput number. Topology changes how much fabric limitation becomes user-visible; 1M concurrency can destroy TTFT and TPOT before KV exhaustion or preemption appears; repeated prefixes can move requests into a very different latency regime; and the useful direction for adding GPUs changes with context. Cross-tool evidence from hardware microbenchmarks, vLLM E2E metrics, scheduler/KV telemetry, Nsight, and PyTorch Profiler can explain these effects, but only when measurement and causal interpretation are kept separate. Standard operational metrics such as GPU utilization or KV% are useful signals, not standalone deployment decisions.”
HERO #1 · TOP 2 · MEASURED & DERIVED
Fabric Exposure Fingerprint
Topology Dictates Transport Risk Under Measured Bandwidth Caps
“The same measured fabric constraint has radically different application impact by topology: at 1M, configured-20G changes TP16/PP1 TTFT by ~+276.7%, while TP4/PP4 changes by only ~+3.9%.”
+276.7% vs +3.9% TTFT

WHAT happened: At 1M context on GCP_CAPPED_20G, TP16/PP1 TTFT explodes from 68.20s to 256.89s (+276.7% degradation; queue wait 0.022s). Under the exact same 20G cap, TP4/PP4 TTFT moves from 28.57s to 29.68s (+3.91% degradation).

WHERE: Multi-node distributed 128K, 512K, and 1M context across GCP_NATIVE (173.6 Gbps) vs Capped 100G (56.8 Gbps) vs Capped 20G (16.5 Gbps).

WHY (Mechanism): TP16/PP1 exposes communication across the VPC network, where transport latency degrades as available bandwidth is restricted. TP4/PP4 restricts cross-node communication to point-to-point pipeline activation exchanges, keeping collective communication intra-node.

DERIVED TRANSPORT-RESPONSE FINGERPRINT: Local fit TTFT(B) = T0 + V_exposed / B. Normalized hidden-width-equivalent exposure coefficient: E_H = V_exposed / (N_tokens * H * b) ≈ 116 hidden-width equivalents (dimensional normalization with H=2304, b=2 bytes BF16; not a literal transfer volume).

DECISION CHANGED: Do not size distributed inference from NIC/iperf capability alone; topology must be characterized under the target network and workload. In this campaign and workload regime, TP4/PP4 exhibited much lower network exposure than TP16/PP1.

BOUNDARY / WHAT IS NOT PROVEN: This is a local empirical sensitivity coefficient over the measured bandwidth range. It is NOT a literal claim that the model physically transmits exactly 116 hidden states per token.
Evidence: HIGH Causal: MED-HIGH
HERO #2 · TOP 3 · MEASURED & DERIVED
Concurrency Value Destruction
Queue Accounting Closure at 1M Extreme Context (Admission / SLO Risk)
“At 1M, added concurrency buys almost no output throughput but destroys user latency. On TP4, c4 adds only ~1.52% output throughput while TTFT becomes 2.48×, TPOT 26.15×, and mean queue residence reaches ~134.43 s.”
+1.52% Output TPS · 2.48× TTFT · 26.15× TPOT · 134.43s Queue
1M TP4/PP1 Closed-Loop c1 → c4 Trade-Off
LoadOutput TPSTTFTTPOTQueue MeanPeak KVPreempt
c=1 (Clean)0.3414793.395 s10.228 ms~0.00 s12.29%0
c=2 (Queued)0.34486 (+0.99%)139.374 s (1.49×)181.974 ms (17.79×)44.340 s15.52%0
c=4 (Severe)0.34666 (+1.52%)231.268 s (2.48×)267.411 ms (26.15×)134.428 s15.51%0
WHAT happened: Moving from c1 to c4 at 1M increases output tokens/s from 0.3415 to 0.3467 (+1.52%). Meanwhile, TTFT balloons from 93.40s to 231.27s (+147.6%), TPOT jumps from 10.23ms to 267.41ms (+2,515%), and mean queue wait reaches 134.43s.

QUEUE ACCOUNTING CLOSURE: Q_closure(c) = [Queue(c) - Queue(c1)] / [TTFT(c) - TTFT(c1)].
• Added TTFT (c4 − c1) = 231.27s − 93.40s = 137.87s. Measured queue wait = 134.43s (97.5% of added TTFT is pure queue residence; preemption delta = 0).
• Independent replication: TP4 c2 ~96.4%, TP4 c4 ~97.5%, TP8 c2 ~95.7%, TP8 c4 ~97.2%.

WHERE: Single-node 1M closed-loop concurrency (c1, c2, c4) on TP4/PP1 and TP8/PP1.

WHY (Mechanism): KV cache remains at only 15.51% (well below OOM limit). Once the severe 1M regime begins, added TTFT numerically tracks queue residence while KV remains far from exhaustion and preemptions stay zero. The detailed service-time/scheduler mechanism behind the queue buildup is not fully decomposed.

DECISION CHANGED: Enforce admission control on queue/TTFT SLO thresholds, NOT on KV cache exhaustion percentage. At 1M context, KV capacity remains far below saturation while latency SLOs are destroyed.

BOUNDARY / WHAT IS NOT PROVEN: Added TTFT is dominated by queue residence; KV remains far from exhaustion; preemptions = 0. Do not collapse TPOT into the same explanation: TPOT degradation is an in-service batching/interference effect after admission whose exclusive root cause requires fine-grained timeline attribution.
Evidence: HIGH Queue Causal: HIGH · TPOT: MED

WHAT happened: In matched TP4/PP4 profiles, full-attention work grows from ~0.30s to ~4.75s (15.7× growth, scaling exponent p_k = ln[W(512K)/W(128K)] / ln(4) ≈ 1.99). Meanwhile, linear KDA recurrence grows ~3.9× (p ≈ 0.99) and MoE routing grows ~3.8× (p ≈ 0.96).

E2E CROSS-CHECK: Native TP4/PP4 c1 TTFT: 128K = 1.709966 s, 512K = 10.221758 s, 1M = 28.567955 s. The E2E curve becomes super-linear, consistent with quadratic attention scaling.

WHERE: Matched valid TP4/PP4 distributed prefill profiles at 128K and 512K.

WHY (Mechanism): The hybrid architecture combines 20 linear KDA layers with 7 full-attention layers. While KDA recurrence scales as O(N), full-attention layers scale as O(N²), causing attention to accumulate GPU work far faster as prompt length scales.

DECISION CHANGED: Do not tune long-context performance from a single 128K profile. Re-evaluate the optimization target as context increases because subsystem pressure scales at different rates. Prioritize FlashAttention & chunk budget for ≥512K; prioritize MoE routing and GEMMs for ≤128K.

BOUNDARY / WHAT IS NOT PROVEN: Do NOT write “Attention becomes the wall-clock critical path at ~420K.” The available profile summaries establish aggregate GPU-work scaling, not exclusive wall-clock critical-path attribution.
Aggregate GPU work != exclusive request wall-clock critical path.

14.8× · 27.9× · 36.0× Speedup

~128K4.8965 s0.3307 s~14.8×917,504 / 1,050,624 = 87.33%

WHAT happened: Hit-conditioned repeat queries reduce 128K median TTFT from 4.897s to 0.331s (14.8×, 87.3% hit ratio); 512K from 32.576s to 1.168s (27.9×, 50.0% hit ratio); 1M from 94.227s to 2.614s (36.0×, 50.0% hit ratio).

WHERE: Single-node TP4 runs (tp4_prefix128k, tp4_prefix512k, tp4_prefix1m).

WHY (Mechanism): Reusing pre-computed KV blocks reuses cached prefix KV state and avoids recomputing the cached prefix portion across the shared prompt prefix. Derived empirical slopes: cold/first TTFT exponent p ≈ 1.4427 (R² ≈ 0.9979); repeat-hit exponent p ≈ 1.0013 (R² ≈ 0.9935).

DECISION CHANGED: Prefix reuse should be treated as a workload-routing/caching lever: workloads with repeated prefixes occupy a fundamentally different latency regime than one-off long prompts. Candidate deployment experiment: Route multi-turn chat and RAG to cache-warm replicas with sticky sessions (workload-dependent benefit; subject to prompt cache residency).

BOUNDARY / WHAT IS NOT PROVEN: Do not recommend prefix caching unconditionally. Empirical exponents describe this measured range, not universal complexity. Production gain depends on reuse frequency, cache residency, eviction, and workload mix.
Evidence: HIGH Causal: MED-HIGH

BOUNDARY / WHAT IS NOT PROVEN: Do not extrapolate this to 512K/1M or another topology without corresponding open-loop sweeps. This is an empirical admission fingerprint, not a universal serving constant.

WHAT happened: Across 4 diagnostic instruments, TP8 incurs an measured decode latency increase over TP4: 16 KiB AllReduce latency is 1.98× higher (19.0 μs vs 37.6 μs); PyTorch Profiler AllReduce Self CUDA time is 3.10× higher (132.3 ms vs 409.9 ms decode-only across 6,985 calls; 18.9 µs vs 58.7 µs/call; prefill step took 119.2ms vs 174.0ms in 55 calls); and 8K c1 TPOT is 41.9% slower (4.475 ms vs 6.350 ms).

WHERE: Single-node 8K decode profiles and serving baselines on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.

WHY (Mechanism): Small-message decode AllReduce collectives are latency-bound. Spanning all 8 GPUs incurs 14-step PCIe ring collective barrier overhead (+17 µs ring; socket crossing ≤ 0.4 µs; thread pinning pending diagnostic).

DECISION CHANGED: Do not assume wider TP improves interactive decode. For interactive short-context decode, prefer TP=4 as candidate deployment topology; TP=8 incurs 14-step PCIe ring collective barrier overhead (+17 µs ring; socket crossing ≤ 0.4 µs; thread pinning pending diagnostic).

BOUNDARY / WHAT IS NOT PROVEN: Nsight aggregate kernel time reflects work volume, not exclusive request critical-path wall time.

WHAT happened: At 1M c4 on TP4, sweeping max_num_seqs across 4, 8, and 16 results in nearly identical TTFTs (232.34s, 232.36s, 232.25s; spread ~0.05%). In the same state, peak_running = 2 and peak_waiting = 3, so the configured ceiling is not reached. Conversely, increasing chunk size from 4K to 16K cuts 1M c1 TTFT from 122.05s to 88.95s (-27.1%).

WHERE: 1M context single-node TP4 scheduler sweeps.

WHY (Mechanism): The configured max_num_seqs ceiling is never reached in the measured state, rendering the knob non-binding. In contrast, changing the chunk/token budget materially changes 1M c1 TTFT, indicating that this control is active in the measured regime; the exact kernel/scheduling mechanism should remain separate from the measured derivative.

DECISION CHANGED: Stop spending optimization effort on max_num_seqs in this measured 1M c4 state; direct tuning effort toward token budget, topology, prefix reuse, and admission where the measured derivative is materially larger.

BOUNDARY / WHAT IS NOT PROVEN: 16K chunk size improves c1 TTFT, but its impact on decode jitter and prefill fairness under mixed traffic remains unresolved.
Evidence: HIGH Causal: MED-HIGH

Busy GPU != Efficient Serving
High Telemetry Utilization Masks Cross-Node Collective Synchronization Stalls
“Higher GPU-utilization telemetry can coexist with substantially worse TTFT. ‘GPU busy’ measures activity, not useful-token efficiency.”
TP16 at 80.6% GPU Util is 2.39× SLOWER than TP4/PP4 at 62.8% Util
1M c1 Serving Telemetry Comparison
TP4 / PP4 (Native Multi-Node)
1M TTFT: 28.57s (62.8% Util)
128K TTFT: 1.71s (35.2% Util)
Pipelined activation transfers maintain lower exposed communication overhead.
TP16 / PP1 (Cross-Node TP)
1M TTFT: 68.20s (80.6% Util)

Communication kernels and collective synchronization loops keep GPUs active without contributing to faster prompt delivery.
WHAT happened: At 1M context on Native fabric, TP16/PP1 reports 80.6% average GPU utilization while delivering 68.20s TTFT. Under the exact same workload, TP4/PP4 reports lower GPU utilization (62.8%) while delivering 28.57s TTFT (2.39× faster). At 128K, TP16/PP1 has 63.2% util and 6.42s TTFT vs TP4/PP4 with 35.2% util and 1.71s TTFT (3.75× faster).

WHERE: Multi-node distributed prefill across 128K and 1M on GCP_NATIVE.

WHY (Mechanism): GPU utilization metrics aggregate communication kernel activity and synchronization loops together with compute, preventing raw utilization percentages from serving as a proxy for useful inference throughput.

DECISION CHANGED: Do not use GPU utilization alone to choose or validate topology or capacity; combine it with TTFT, TPOT/goodput, queue residence, communication exposure, and profiler composition.

BOUNDARY / WHAT IS NOT PROVEN: Do not fit a causal regression from four topology points. Do not interpret high utilization as bad. The correct statement is: GPU utilization is semantically incomplete because communication kernels also count as GPU activity.
Evidence: HIGH Causal: MEDIUM

1. Fabric Exposure

Topology Dependent

The same measured fabric constraint produces radically different user-visible TTFT damage depending on topology.

Key Measured Finding 1M · configured-20G vs GCP_NATIVE

Why It Matters
Fabric capability alone does not determine serving impact. The scale-out topology determines how much transport degradation is exposed to application TTFT. Network sizing must be driven by measured application exposure, not raw NIC/iperf bandwidth alone.

Secondary Evidence
Key Architectural Takeaways
  • Fabric sensitivity varies dramatically by topology: scale-out design cannot be treated as a single uniform class.
  • TP16/PP1 is severely exposed to transport degradation because AllReduce collectives are serialized over the cross-node fabric on every layer (+188.69s tax @ 1M).
  • TP4/PP4 is far less sensitive in the same 1M cap condition (+3.91% TTFT) because cross-node boundaries use point-to-point Send/Recv pipelining.
  • Small negative TP8/PP2 deltas (-0.10% @ 1M) are signed observations; do not call them noise without replicate variance.
⚡ Architectural Decision Changed
Choose and size scale-out topology from measured application exposure to transport degradation, not NIC/iperf capability alone.
Boundary: No 8K application cap sweep; no 50G/10G application claim; configured network label != measured achieved bandwidth; no universal topology winner.

PCI Bus & Socket Mapping (from node inventory): GPUs 0–3 sit on Socket 0 (PCI buses 05/06/0A/0B); GPUs 4–7 sit on Socket 1 (PCI buses 84/85/89/8A). For TP4/PP2, manifests force GPUs 0–3 per node (both stages sit entirely on Socket 0 of their respective node). TP4/PP4 uses four TP4 stages (2 stages per node across sockets); TP8/PP2 spans both sockets within each node.
🔬 Repeatability Noise Floor (§4.11): Eight pairs of identical configurations across the campaign establish the empirical dashboard noise floor: TTFT agrees within 0.03–0.5% at c1 and within 1.9–3.9% under load (8K c8, 128K c4); TPOT agrees within 0.02–2.1%. Deltas of ±0.10% (e.g. TP8/PP2 at 1M: −0.10%, or TP4/PP2 at 1M under 100G: +0.13%) are within pure replicate noise; +1.14% (TP4/PP2 at 20G, 1M) is at the statistical boundary; +3.91% (TP4/PP4 at 20G, 1M) and +14.67% (TP4/PP4 at 20G, 128K) are empirically verified network slowdowns.

Key Findings: (1) TP4/PP4 at 1M is both fastest (28.57s) and lowest energy (143.1 J/ktok). (2) Power reveals true work: TP16 at 80.6% "utilization" draws 225 W (busy spinning on AllReduce sync) while TP4/PP4 at 62.8% draws 310 W (real compute). (3) In every PP layout, Node 1 draws 17–21% more power than Node 0 at 1M (414 vs 343 W, 337 vs 282 W, 289 vs 247 W) because later stages hold more full-attention layers (§4.7).

Profiles from profiles_multi_node_native/tp4_pp4_dist/long_prefill_512k (16 usable ranks, grouped by AllReduce counts 1,143 / 1,067 / 1,067 / 915 = stages 0–3; 27 layers split 7/7/7/6). Corrected in v1.1.

v1.1 Correction & Cost Model: Equal layer counts ≠ equal work when attention cost scales with context! The 7 full-attention layers sit at #3, #7, #11, #15, #19, #23, #26. A two-parameter cost model (0.61s/layer + 2.36s/full-attn layer at 512K) reproduces measured busy time of every stage within 5% (model: 6.6 / 9.0 / 9.0 / 8.4s vs measured 6.3 / 9.1 / 8.9 / 8.5s). Because full-attention layers sit every 4th layer, any contiguous partition of ≥ 8 layers picks up two attention layers; stage 0 cannot absorb an 8th layer without picking up layer #7. Testing all 2,600 contiguous splits of 27 layers into 4 reveals none beats 7/7/7/6 (partition 8,7,6,6 makes stage 0 heaviest and increases TTFT by +7%). The 26% stage-0 idle is structural for PP4 and must be priced, not tuned. Where gain exists: In PP2, partition 15,12 (vs default 14,13) cuts stage-0 idle 10% → 3% and shortens 512K TTFT by 3.5% on TP4/PP2!
Independent Confirmation (PP2 Check — §6.2): The two PP2 128K captures independently confirm the 3:4 attention split predicted by the layer map: Stage 0 / Stage 1 flash attention time ratio is 0.77 on TP4/PP2 (8 usable ranks) and 0.77 on TP8/PP2 (15 usable ranks), closely corroborating (within 3% of 0.75) the 0.75 ratio expected from the 3 vs 4 full-attention layer distribution (of 7 total layers: #3, #7, #11 vs #15, #19, #23, #26).

Production admission limits depend on explicit application SLOs; c=1 is the cleanest measured single-node operating point.

Four Critical Readings: (1) Single requests never queue; engine accounting closes to within 6% (vLLM overhead is only 14 ms at 8K and grows with prompt length due to tokenization/transfer). (2) First token is collective-bound for short prompts (54% on TP4, 75% on TP16) and kernel-bound for long ones (74–83% at 512K–1M). (3) Under load, wall time is scheduler-dominated: queueing is 50% of first token at 128K c4 and 58% at 1M c4; waiting behind other requests' prefills is 86–96% of decode time at long contexts. (4) 1M decode is 54% memory-speed KV read across all widths; PP2 pays 5–6% at stage boundary vs 12–13% for PP4; TP16 cross-node collective is ~208 µs/call.

🔍 Architectural Discovery: FP8 KV-Cache Compatibility on Blackwell Workstations
Resolution of the V8 `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` assertion failure on dual-node NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Ada/Blackwell.
ROOT-CAUSE AUDITED

Upstream Engine Invariant: In vllm/model_executor/layers/attention/mla_attention.py, vLLM strictly validates backend_supports_prefill_query_quantization():

if not current_platform.is_device_capability_family(100):
    return False # Strictly requires GB200/B200 SM100 Architecture

1. Hardware Generation: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 is Blackwell workstation architecture (SM120, capability 12.0). Because is_device_capability_family(100) strictly returns False, vLLM rejects prefill query quantization.
2. MLA Head Dimensions: Kimi-Linear-48B uses Multi-Head Latent Attention with head dimensions (192, 64, 256). FlashInfer only supports (128, 64, 128), TRT-LLM Ragged lacks SM120 binaries, and FlashAttention-4 supports BF16/FP16 only.
3. Conclusion: FP8 KV-Cache for Kimi-Linear-48B strictly requires NVIDIA GB200 datacenter hardware. The V8 failure was not a deployment error or runtime bug, but an authoritative hardware microarchitecture boundary.

>
⚡ Chunk-Size / Prompt Budget Finding (8K at c4)
The 8K first token doubles at c4 (0.21s → 0.42s own prefill) while queue is only 27 ms. Because prompt length (8,192) equals max_num_batched_tokens, a single active decode token forces the prompt into a 2nd chunk that waits behind the next prompt's first chunk. Expanding batch token headroom to 8,448 (or prompting with 8,000 tokens) is predicted to save ~211 ms (plan A1 test).
🧠 MoE Decode Batching & Expert Expansion Finding
Under load, MoE decode step expands from 4.5 ms (c1, 8 active experts) to 15.8 ms (c32, ~163 of 256 experts expected under uniform routing) and 22.9 ms at full load (~222 experts). Routed weights read at memory speed grow from 0.9 ms to 10.5 and 14.9 ms, while kernels above the floor stay at 2.5–4.8 ms. By c16, decode is memory-bound on weights rather than KV, explaining why throughput scales sub-linearly with concurrency.
🛑 Decode Stalls Behind Other Requests' Prefill Chunks — How Much of Per-Token Wait is Interference (§4.5)
Campaign Scope: Single-node local execution (TP4/PP1 & TP8/PP1). Distributed layouts (TP4/PP2, TP8/PP2, TP4/PP4, TP16/PP1) were run at c=1 only; concurrency / multi-request load not yet measured in this campaign.
Per-token inter-token latencies (itls list in benchmark JSONs; first entry skipped). A "stall" is an ITL > 100 ms. Co-scheduled prefills freeze ongoing decodes for exactly one chunk duration.

Architectural Takeaway: Quantifies the prefill/decode disaggregation case without new experiments: at 8K load, decode SLO is dictated by prefill chunk interference, not batch compute. Explains the chunk size trade-off: 16K chunks at 128K c4 gave lower mean TPOT (105 vs 141 ms) because there were half as many stall interruptions! Remedies: decode-priority scheduling, separate P/D pools, or admission control gated by "prefill chunks in flight".

Scale-Out Scheduler Discovery: Pipeline Parallelism (TP4/PP4) is verified by empirical token pool scaling: TP4/PP1 8.14M, TP8/PP1 8.21M, TP16/PP1 8.24M, TP4/PP2 16.9M, TP8/PP2 17.0M, TP4/PP4 36.4M tokens (MLA latent KV cache 8,064 B/token replicated across TP ranks; headroom = 10% vLLM reserve), reducing 1M context peak KV cache usage to just 2.748% (vs 12.129% on TP16/PP1 and 12.290% on TP4/PP1). Queue wait remains below 0.00004s across all scale-out c1 points (~0.000038s on TP8/PP2 1M) with zero preemptions.

Memory Attribution Note: Total GPU Peak Memory remains ~86.7–88.8 GiB across 96 GiB GPUs while KV utilization varies; the exact allocator breakdown is not directly measured here. KV cache consumes only 0.365% to 12.129% of dedicated KV cache capacity.
⚠️ Client-Side Concurrency Cap Caveat (§4.13): tp4_openloop_8192 ran with --max-concurrency 64, and tp4_openloop_131072 with --max-concurrency 32. Achieved request rate saturates at 3.30–3.42 req/s (8K) and 0.183–0.185 req/s (128K) from 0.90× onward while offered rate climbs to 5.29 / 0.285 req/s. The excess requests queue in the benchmark client, invisible to server-side TTFT. Consequently, server queue_mean stays ≤ 0.25 s, 8K TTFT shows non-monotonicity above the knee (979 → 784 → 826 ms), and the real unconstrained cliff is steeper than shown. (The knee location at 0.90× / 0.75× remains empirically sound as it occurs below the client cap).

📍 Capacity Knee / Admission Decision
Candidate Knee location (Heuristic: slope inflection of TPOT / queue degradation)8K: ~0.90x offered load (~3.811 RPS offered, ~3.302 req/s achieved; queue 0.182s, TPOT 60.86ms) · 128K: ~0.75x offered load (~0.171 RPS; queue 1.94s, TPOT 50.57ms)
Leading Measured Operating Point (SLO Objective Dependent)8K: c≤8 closed-loop (TPOT 10.82ms, queue 0.19s) · 128K: ≤0.75x offered load (~0.171 RPS, TTFT 6.94s, queue 1.94s) · 1M: c=1 cleanest measured point (TTFT 74.89s TP8 / 93.25s TP4, queue ~0.00s)
What breaks firstQueue wait time and TPOT degrade simultaneously before memory exhaustion: at 1M c2 queue reaches 35.3s (TP8) / 44.3s (TP4) and TPOT increases to 177.2ms / 182.0ms while KV (15.3–15.5%) and preemptions (0) remain stable
DecisionWorkload-scoped candidate admission limits: for 1M interactive/SLO workloads, admit at c=1 (cleanest measured single-node point); for 8K interactive decode, evaluate c≤8 to keep TPOT ~10.8ms depending on target SLO; for 128K open-loop, evaluate throttling admission beyond candidate knee 0.75× (~0.171 RPS) prior to the 1.00× queuing cliff.

🔍 Measurement, Model Bounds & Attribution (§7 v1.2)
Totals are measured on every row: client first-token / inter-token time, engine queue, and prefill duration histograms.
Loaded Attribution: Engine decode time matches client (e2e − first token) within 0.4% across all loaded runs. Residual outside queue + prefill is real time outside the engine core. Normal decode step is median token with ITL ≤ 100 ms; remainder is prefill contention delay.
Additive Scope Note: This 4-chart panel is strictly additive; kernel composition cards, torch profiles, and eager baselines remain untouched. Distributed layouts (TP4/PP2, TP8/PP2, TP4/PP4, TP16/PP1) were run at c1 only; loaded points exist on TP4/PP1 and TP8/PP1.
🌊 Technical Clarification on "Waves" (§7)
1. vLLM V1 Engine Waves (DP/EP Coordination): In vLLM V1, a wave coordinates data-parallel workers with expert parallelism via lockstep steps and dummy forward passes. This campaign ran DP = 1, EP = 1 (see Evidence tab), so no dummy-step or lockstep waves existed.
2. GPU Kernel SM Wave Quantization: Tail wave SM under-utilization at small batch (e.g. GEMV running at 43% memory bandwidth) lives inside the "kernels above memory floor" segment, not beside it (requires NCU targeted profiling).

🧭 Empirical Profiler Observations → Workload-Scoped Architectural Takeaways
Causal mechanisms directly substantiated by Nsight SQLite kernel tables & PyTorch call logs
ACTIONABLE DEPLOYMENT RULES
Empirical ObservationCross-Validated Mechanism / ContributorWorkload-Scoped Candidate TakeawaySupporting Artifact
TP4 Decode beats TP8 (-29.5% TPOT @ 8K c1) Canonical matched 8K context baseline: TP4 4.475ms vs TP8 6.350ms (TP4 ~29.5% lower TPOT). Under graphs-on serving, TP8 14-step ring AllReduce barrier latency increases to 58.7 µs vs 18.9 µs on TP4 (3.23 ms vs 1.04 ms collective budget; +17 µs from longer ring, socket crossing adds ≤ 0.4 µs), canceling out GEMV speedup. Single-Node Interactive Serving: For interactive decode serving: Co-locating TP4 workers within a single socket/ring avoids 14-step ring AllReduce latency; CPU thread pinning (numactl/taskset) across dual sockets is pending diagnostic. profiles_torch_single_node/ (graphs-on torch profiles)
TP8 Prefill beats TP4 (-12% @ 512K, -20% @ 1M) At 512K, TTFT drops from 31.92s to 28.09s (-12.0%) and at 1M from 93.25s to 74.89s (-19.9%). Note: At 128K, TP8 is slightly slower than TP4 in serving (4.81s vs 4.53s). TP8 reduces measured FlashAttention kernel duration in captured profile (6.24ms to 4.26ms). Single-Node Batch / Document Ingestion: For long-context prefill workloads (512K+), evaluate TP8 where prompt processing latency dominates. tp8_prefill/cuda_gpu_kern_sum.csv
TP4/PP4 Dist beats TP16/PP1 (2.4x speedup @ 1M) Pipeline Parallelism transmits sequential activations via P2P SendRecv (8.3% of stage work). TP16 ranks show high aggregate AllReduce kernel-work share (76.2% in captured profile). 27 hidden layers (20 KDA, 7 full attention). Multi-Node Cloud Deployment: For multi-node cloud deployments on TCP/IP VPC, candidate topology favors Pipeline Parallelism (TP4/PP4 or TP8/PP2) over cross-node Tensor Parallelism (TP16) for tested workloads. tp4_pp4_dist/prefill_128k vs tp16_pp1_dist/prefill_128k
Flat 1M c4 max_num_seqs (~232.3s) TTFT is flat across max_num_seqs 4/8/16 (~232.3s) and peak_running never approaches those configured ceilings; max_num_seqs is non-binding in this tested regime. Tuning Discipline: Do not spend time tuning scheduler sequence limits on extreme-context workloads when running below ceiling. Optimize prompt chunk size and enable prefix reuse. tp4_1m_maxseq4..16/bench.json
Host Launch Gap (3.47s in cudaLaunchKernel) CPU driver launch overhead averages 3.9 μs per kernel; across 888,504 kernel launches, host scheduling overhead accumulates to 31.2% of CPU time. Runtime Optimization: Serving already operates with CUDA Graphs ON (4.47 ms decode step vs 30.5 ms in eager profiler). tp4_decode/cuda_api_sum.csv

🚀 Server Cold Start & Model Loading Telemetry (§4.12)
server_ready − server_start in every case_manifest.json across 77 runs. Answers model loading, disk-to-VRAM copy, and CUDA graph capture overhead.
STARTUP TELEMETRY
Topology / ConfigurationStartup Duration (server_start → server_ready)First-Request TTFT OverheadWeight per GPUMechanism & Resource Bottleneck
TP4 / PP1 (26 cases)128–192 s (Median: 138 s)0–3.4% of median24.5 GB / GPUSlowest loading: 24.5 GB weights loaded per GPU, 4 GPUs in parallel; graph capture scales per GPU.
TP8 / PP144–52 s0–2.8% of median12.2 GB / GPUWeights halved to 12.2 GB/GPU; 8 GPUs read in parallel, cutting loading time by ~65%.
TP4 / PP4 & TP8 / PP244–52 s0–2.5% of median6.1–12.2 GB / GPUMulti-node pipeline stages load in parallel across both nodes.
TP16 / PP1 (Cross-node TP)44–52 s (Cold page cache: 110s)+3.4% (First request)6.1 GB / GPUFast weight loading, but first request experiences +3.4% cold-start prologue across VPC.
Campaign Summary: Over the whole campaign, 1.25 hours of 4.92 hours of total server-up time was start-up and CUDA-graph compilation (25%). The first request after server-ready (with warmups = 0 on 77 runs) exhibits at most 0–3.4% latency penalty relative to steady-state median — confirming that CUDA graph capture and compilation occur entirely before server_ready.

Derived Decision-Intelligence Build Layer
Frontend should consume evidence-backed analysis outputs rather than re-derive conclusions ad hoc
DEPLOYMENT_FINDINGS.jsonobservation · interpretation · confidence · implication · evidence
BOTTLENECK_REGIME_MAP.csvcontext/load/phase bottleneck evidence
TUNING_SENSITIVITY.csvhigh/medium/low-sensitivity knobs
SLO_CAPACITY_ENVELOPE.csvthroughput/latency/queue capacity knee
SCALEOUT_NATIVE_FABRIC.csvnative topology/context metrics
SCALEOUT_NETWORK_COVERAGE.mdrecords multi-node network sensitivity findings across native and capped sweeps
TOPOLOGY_WORKLOAD_MATRIX.csvworkload-scoped topology evidence
DASHBOARD_DATA_CONTRACT.jsonstable UI schema / provenance
Provenance / Statistical Guardrails
Baseline vs Performance Characterization: never silently merge. Every row carries suite_version, run_id, model revision, runtime version, network provenance and evidence class. Compare only sufficiently matched workloads.
Percentiles: promote p95 only when completed sample count ≥ 20; promote p99 only when completed sample count ≥ 100. Raw low-N percentile fields may exist but must not be presented as reliable SLO statistics.
Evidence classes: DIRECT_MEASURED · TIMELINE_ATTRIBUTED · DERIVED · UNRESOLVED.
Runtime Dashboard Acceptance
Read FINAL_VALIDATION first
Join coverage + metrics
Keep 7 top-level tabs
GCP_NATIVE primary + configured-100G/20G auxiliary measured
128K/512K/1M scale-out
4 distributed topologies
TP4/TP8 1M c1/c2/c4
1M scheduler / FP8-KV / prefix
p95/p99 sample gating
No invented profiler %
Both-node telemetry visible
Every point traceable
Every chart exposes full TP/PP config identity
Scheduler/KV charts expose exact TP/PP per series
Profiler rows expose exact TP/PP per trace
Distributed profiler matrix lists all four topologies explicitly
Evidence rows preserve complete configuration identity
